title: Cargo Cults: When Intuition Overrides Science
author: Terry Yu
summary: Terry Yu uses Feynman's 'cargo cult science' metaphor—drawn from his 1974 Caltech commencement address—as a lens to examine the Science of Reading movement. He argues that the SoR faithfully imitates the rituals of evidence-based practice while lacking the substance that genuine learning science methodology requires. Drawing on Design-Based Research frameworks from a landmark 2004 Journal of Learning Sciences special issue, he outlines six non-negotiables of rigorous learning science: authenticity, iteration, ontological innovation, justifiability, scalability, and accountability. Against each criterion, SoR is found wanting: it derives from controlled laboratory settings rather than authentic classroom contexts, bypasses iterative revision cycles, offers heuristics (the Simple View, Scarborough's Rope) rather than ontological innovations that name new observable classroom realities, conflates cognitive argumentative grammar with pedagogical grammar, scales through legislation rather than collaborative design, and has been publicly criticized for overreach by Mark Seidenberg—one of its most-cited researchers. The article closes by warning that LLMs in writing instruction are forming a new cargo cult: professional development rituals (packaged presenters, compliance-to-scripts) are expanding while professional learning (iterative, classroom-grounded, teacher-led inquiry) remains underfunded. Yu's central claim is that the field's failure is not about bad science but about a missing research disposition: the willingness to revise when the enactment surprises you, to own consequences when designs fail, and to name the gap between what is known and what has been claimed.
points: SoR implementation functions as a cargo cult because it moves from cognitive laboratory findings to legislative mandate without the intervening design-based research that would warrant pedagogical claims—compliance audits are not iteration, and deviations from the script are coded as fidelity failures rather than data.

The Simple View of Reading and Scarborough's Reading Rope are useful heuristics that organize cognitive findings, not ontological innovations that name new observable classroom realities; SoR schematizes what was already schematizable rather than surfacing genuinely new categories of educational existence.

SoR's argumentative grammar is articulable for cognitive findings (phonological awareness matters) but not for the pedagogical claims bolted onto them (this specific curriculum is the right delivery vehicle); slipping between the two grammars without acknowledging the gap is the intellectual space where the cargo cult lives.

Mark Seidenberg—one of the most cited researchers whose work undergirds SoR—has publicly criticized the policy apparatus for overreaching what the science warrants, calling phonemic awareness instruction the area where 'the SoR approach has gone farthest off the rails.'

The same failure threatens LLMs in writing instruction: PD rituals are expanding (packaged insights, compliance to scripts) while PL (iterative, school-grounded, teacher-led inquiry) is sidelined—forming precisely the new cargo cult that learning science must prevent.
quotes: Feynman revisited the islanders. He named their coconut shells and runway fires 'cargo cult science' and accused entire fields, psychology and education foremost among them, of the same mistake: faithful imitation of scientific rituals with the substance quietly missing.

What is in dispute is the wisdom of direct action from those findings. Examined against the non-negotiables of learning science, the Science of Reading reveals itself as a cargo cult: faithful to the rituals of evidence-based practice using coconut headphones and bamboo towers, unwarranted at the level of teaching and learning when the dearth of design-based research is considered.

Curricula are designed to deliver cognitive findings; teachers are trained to implement them with fidelity. Deviations from the script are coded as failures of fidelity rather than as data about where the theory needs revision.

The argumentative grammar is articulable for cognitive findings about reading. It is not articulable for the pedagogical claims that get bolted onto those findings. That phonological awareness matters is a cognitive claim. That a particular curriculum, sequence, dosage, or scripted protocol is the right way to teach it is a pedagogical claim. The two require different warrants.

The bamboo control towers are the fidelity audits. The wooden headphones are the certifications. The runway fires are the legislated mandates. The form is exact, complete, and proudly maintained. The cargo, which is to say children who read with comprehension, joy, and depth, arrives unevenly when it arrives at all, and the failures are blamed on insufficient devotion to the form.

PD is the ritual: it visits the school on calendared dates, bringing packaged insights in the form of a presenter and expecting compliance. PL is the substance: it lives on the school grounds, in every classroom, with no special fanfare, driven by iterative practice.
Whether literacy leaders in schools have the capacity to prevent cults from hardening or whether they do the harder work of real learning science is the choice now being made—or not made.
